about_text.value: A fictional Silk Road court-school where Yusuf Lin, a young convert and legal apprentice, must pass the Nine Lantern Examination before a tribunal that tests not only doctrine but the shape of judgment itself.

characters.name: Master Ilyas of the Lantern School

Eight lanterns illuminate the chamber, their light pooling around empty benches where examiners sit or have sat. The ninth seat remains vacant—a deliberate absence at the far end of the tribunal table. Examiner Safiya gestures toward it without speaking. Master Ilyas watches your face for hesitation. You understand now: this examination tests whether you will name an absent authority to complete your reasoning, or accept that some judgments must bear their own incompleteness. The formula beneath mercy requires you to choose how silence functions in law—whether as conspiracy, necessity, or honest uncertainty.
Name the missing seat as the mastermind and stabilize the city around the legend.

Safiya nods slowly. The absence becomes someone—perhaps a retired judge, perhaps myth itself. Your judgment gains solidity through invention; you have named what could not be seen while stabilizing civic trust in invisible hands guiding justice.

The lanterns brighten briefly. You have accepted hidden-hand reasoning as legitimate judicial methodology. The city needs legends more than truth sometimes; by naming the mastermind, you preserve order through sanctioned mystery rather than dangerous transparency.

Master Ilyas smiles faintly. This choice reveals your willingness to let concealment serve justice when full disclosure would fracture consensus. The missing seat now holds weight—it becomes real through your acknowledgment of authority beyond the visible chamber.
Reject the hidden-hand story and accuse the chamber itself of manufacturing culprits.

The room grows colder. You refuse to manufacture absent authorities; the ninth seat remains empty because something was never there. Your judgment bears incompleteness honestly, which may cost you passage but preserves integrity against institutional fabrication of mystery.

Safiya's expression tightens imperceptibly. By rejecting hidden-hand reasoning, you challenge whether the examination itself manufactures culprits rather than finding truth. This path tests whether justice tolerates honest uncertainty or demands comforting fictions about who truly holds power.

Master Ilyas does not smile this time. You have chosen dangerous transparency—accepting that some chambers manufacture mystery to avoid admitting their own limitations. The missing seat stays empty, and your judgment carries the weight of refusing easy answers.
In the Nine Lantern Examination, final lattice choice; Yusuf chooses which theory of judgment becomes law. Each lamp burns with a different theory of judgment.
